title: VPNs & Perimeter Security Basics
summary: Understand what a VPN actually gives you, how site-to-site and remote-access tunnels differ, and where a VPN ends and a firewall begins.

slides.subTitle: The encrypted tunnel
slides.markdown:
A **VPN** builds an **encrypted tunnel** across a network you don't trust — usually the public Internet. Each end wraps (encapsulates) your real packets inside encrypted ones, so anyone in the middle sees ciphertext, not your data or its real destination.

![Two sites joined by an encrypted VPN tunnel across the Internet](assets/vpn-tunnel.svg)

The key idea: a VPN changes *who can read the traffic on the path*, not *who is allowed to send it*. That second job belongs to a firewall.

assets.alt: Two sites joined by an encrypted VPN tunnel across the Internet

slides.subTitle: Two deployment shapes
slides.markdown:
VPNs come in two shapes. A **site-to-site** VPN permanently joins two networks — e.g. a branch office to headquarters — through gateway devices; users on either side never run VPN software, the routers do the tunneling. A **remote-access** VPN connects one device — a laptop on hotel Wi-Fi — into a corporate network, using client software on that device.

Rule of thumb: site-to-site glues **networks** together; remote-access plugs a single **user** in. A company typically runs both at once.

slides.subTitle: IPsec vs TLS-based
slides.markdown:
**IPsec** VPNs operate at the network layer (Layer 3), encrypting whole IP packets. They're the classic choice for always-on site-to-site links, but need matching config on both ends and can be blocked by NAT and strict firewalls.

**TLS-based** VPNs (e.g. OpenVPN, or clientless SSL portals) ride over TLS on a normal port like 443, so they traverse firewalls and NAT easily and suit remote users on messy networks. The trade-off: IPsec is leaner and kernel-integrated; TLS VPNs are more firewall-friendly and easier to deploy per-user.

slides.subTitle: Three filtering depths
slides.markdown: A **firewall** decides which traffic is *allowed*, at one of three depths. A **packet-filtering** firewall checks each packet's header (IP, port, protocol) in isolation — fast, but blind to context. A **stateful** firewall tracks connections, so it allows return traffic for sessions it saw start and drops unsolicited packets. An **application-layer** firewall (proxy) inspects the payload — HTTP paths, TLS SNI — to enforce app-level rules. Deeper inspection adds context but costs more per packet. See [network hardware](network-hardware-topologies).

slides.subTitle: A remote worker's path
slides.markdown:
Follow a remote worker: their laptop's VPN client encrypts traffic and sends it across home Wi-Fi and the public Internet to the company's **VPN concentrator**. The concentrator decrypts it and forwards it onto the internal network as if the laptop were physically in the office.

![A remote worker's traffic tunneled through a VPN into the corporate network](assets/remote-worker-vpn.svg)

This is why VPN access feels like being "on the network" — and why a compromised laptop is dangerous: the tunnel carries it straight inside.

assets.alt: A remote worker's traffic tunneled through a VPN into the corporate network

slides.subTitle: VPN vs firewall
slides.markdown:
They're often confused because both sit at the network edge, but they answer different questions.

| | VPN | Firewall |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Can this path be read? | Is this traffic allowed? |
| Action | Encrypts + tunnels traffic | Permits or blocks traffic |
| Protects | Confidentiality on an untrusted path | The network from unwanted flows |
| If removed | Traffic sent in the clear | Anything can reach inside |

How to decide: use a VPN when data crosses a network you don't control; use a firewall to control *what* may enter or leave. Most designs need both — a VPN with no firewall behind it just delivers attackers securely.
